Clement VII. Born Giulio de' Medici, a cousin of Pope Leo X, he reigned as pope from 1523 to 1534. His pontificate was tumultuous, defined by the rapid spread of the Protestant Reformation and intense geopolitical conflicts. He struggled to navigate the rivalry between France and the Holy Roman Empire, leading to the catastrophic Sack of Rome.

He was the illegitimate son of Giuliano de' Medici, who was assassinated in the Pazzi Conspiracy, and was later legitimized by his cousin Leo X. His refusal to annul the marriage of King Henry VIII of England to Catherine of Aragon triggered the English Reformation. He refused primarily because he was under the physical control of Catherine's nephew, Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. During the Sack of Rome in 1527, he was trapped in the Castel Sant'Angelo but managed to escape through the Passetto di Borgo when mutinous troops of Emperor Charles V pillaged the city.

Clement joined the League of Cognac in 1526 with France, Venice, Florence, and Milan to challenge the expanding imperial power of Charles V in Italy. He commissioned Michelangelo to paint The Last Judgment on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel shortly before his death.
